prompt.context: Scotty's is a fast food restaurant chain with over 2,000 stores in the US, mostly concentrated in the South. Restaurants are structured as old-fashioned drive-ins — each store has 20 to 30 drive-in spots where patrons can order and receive their food while seated in their cars. The stores have no seating areas. The menu can be broken down into 3 categories: (1) Main courses: Burger, fried chicken; (2) Sodas: Over 300 varieties, some proprietary; (3) Desserts: Milkshakes and other ice cream desserts. During the first 20 years of operations, Scotty's business grew steadily. However, Scotty's business declined last year. Their CEO has hired McKinsey to determine a growth strategy for the business.
prompt.question: Given this information, brainstorm some initial ideas on a growth strategy for Scotty's.

clarifying_info.q: Are the pilot restaurants in the same regions as standard stores?
clarifying_info.a: The case does not specify — treat as comparable for analysis purposes.

clarifying_info.q: What does the data on pilot stores show?
clarifying_info.a: The interviewer will show you exhibit data on pilot restaurant performance vs. standard restaurants when ready to proceed to that part.

exhibits.title: Standard vs. Pilot Restaurant Performance
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of standard restaurants and pilot restaurants, showing price per item, quantity sold, and profit margin for each menu category (Burgers, Sodas, Milkshakes).
exhibits.data: Standard Restaurants — Burgers: price $2, qty 15,000, margin 15%; Sodas: price $2, qty 10,000, margin 10%; Milkshakes: price $4, qty 5,000, margin 20%. Pilot Restaurants — Burgers: price $2, qty ~15,000, margin ~15%; Sodas: price $2, qty ~10,000, margin ~10%; Milkshakes: price $5, qty ~10,000, margin ~25%.

framework: Store footprint and profitability: assess store placement, open new stores, close unprofitable ones, or adopt a franchise model
Revenue — customer side: grow customer base, target most profitable segments
Revenue — product side: review pricing, product mix, and differentiation; 300+ soda varieties may be excessive relative to distribution/inventory cost
Costs — fixed and variable: raw material costs given high SKU variety, distribution costs with multiple soda suppliers, storage costs from complex product mix
Competitive landscape: performance in high-density vs. low-competition markets
Pilot model evaluation: compare seated-area pilot stores vs. standard drive-in stores on revenue, margin, and customer behavior

questions.prompt: What are your initial impressions of the exhibit comparing standard vs. pilot restaurants? What are the benefits and drawbacks of the pilot model?
questions.guidance: Strong answers note: milkshake price increased in pilots AND volume doubled — unusual combination suggesting the seated environment drives additional purchases (customers buy milkshakes as a second transaction while sitting and socializing). Sodas and burgers are priced the same in pilots, suggesting mark-up potential. Pilot stores do higher overall volume. Drawback: higher build-out cost for seating areas; potential brand-identity shift away from drive-in nostalgia.

questions.prompt: The client thinks their milkshake business has a lot of potential. How many soda sales would a standard restaurant have to convert to milkshake sales in order to increase their total profit margin to 20%?
questions.guidance: Candidate must compute current overall revenue and profit, find the gap to 20% margin, then solve for the number of conversions using the marginal profit difference per unit between a soda and a milkshake.

math.setup: Standard store revenues and profits by category; find x = number of sodas converted to milkshakes so that total profit / total revenue = 20%.
steps: Total revenue = $70,000; total profit = $10,500; current margin = 15%
Target profit at 20% margin on $70,000 revenue = $14,000
math.answer: Approximately 5,833 soda sales must be converted to milkshake sales to reach a 20% overall profit margin.

brainstorming.prompt: Brainstorm a growth strategy for Scotty's covering store operations, revenue levers, cost levers, and competitive positioning.

categories.name: Store footprint
ideas: Open new stores in underserved geographies
Close or remodel chronically unprofitable locations
Franchise model to accelerate expansion with lower capital outlay
Convert some standard drive-ins to the pilot seated model

categories.name: Revenue — pricing and product
ideas: Increase milkshake prices at standard stores (pilot data shows low price elasticity for milkshakes)
Rationalize soda menu from 300+ to top-selling varieties to reduce complexity
Bundle promotions to increase average ticket
Introduce seasonal or limited-time items to drive traffic

categories.name: Revenue — customer
ideas: Target families and groups who benefit from seated dining (pilot insight)
Loyalty program to increase visit frequency
Catering or delivery to expand revenue beyond in-store visits

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Reduce soda SKUs to lower procurement, distribution, and storage costs
Consolidate suppliers for better volume pricing
Optimize staffing levels based on peak traffic patterns

categories.name: Competitive positioning
ideas: Lean into milkshake and proprietary soda differentiation as brand identity
Benchmark performance in high-competition vs. low-competition markets to identify white space
Assess whether drive-in nostalgia is a defensible position or a growth constraint

recommendation: Shift from the standard drive-in model toward the pilot seated-area model, which drives both higher milkshake volumes and higher overall revenue
Within existing standard restaurants, convert soda sales to milkshake sales — approximately 5,833 unit conversions per store are needed to reach a 20% profit margin
risks: Capital investment required to convert or build seated-format restaurants
Risk of brand-identity dilution if drive-in nostalgia is a core differentiator for existing customers
Milkshake substitution from sodas assumes fungible demand — may not fully materialize in all markets
next_steps: Conduct consumer research to validate milkshake demand elasticity and optimal price point at standard stores
Model unit economics for pilot-format conversion cost vs. incremental revenue benefit
Evaluate franchise model feasibility to fund expansion without full capital outlay
Explore soda SKU rationalization and quantify cost savings from supplier consolidation
